summary: Capitalism, divergence and industrialisation. A new Debate entry gathers five components (the transition debate; the Brenner debate and political Marxism; explaining industrialisation; the Great Divergence; slavery and capitalism) in eleven strands, with a roster of named participants and readers and a dated chronology from 1944 to 2023 (Toynbee 1884 as context). Robert Brenner and Ellen Meiksins Wood become person entries. Fields and person entries feed the debate (marx, Dobb, Hilton, Brenner, Wood, historicalecon, economic, demography, consumption, technology, global, dependency, historicalsociology, Williams, atlantic, and Pomeranz's 2011 timing reassessment as Vries reports it) and critics answer within it (the debate against Brenner and Wood; quant against the new history of capitalism). Brenner's own critiques (of Postan's demographic model, Le Roy Ladurie, Frank and Wallerstein, and Pomeranz) and influences (Marx, Dobb, Tawney's and Hilton's evidence, Hill as read by Wood and Gentles) are drawn on his entry; Wood's (Brenner, Thompson; against Cohen and anti-Eurocentric world history) on hers. edge_1050 (critics of Pomeranz) and edge_407 (Drescher on Williams) move from economic to the debate, with Brenner and Isett split out of edge_1050; no strand is moved.

rationale: Research of 2026-10-18: data/extension-2026/capitalism-debate-2026-10-18/ (components 3–5) and data/extension-2026/brenner-2026-10-18/ (components 1–2, Brenner, Wood). Every edge rests on a read text in the author's own words or a named reader's explicit statement; publisher excerpts, abstracts, Cambridge Core openings, WebFetch extractions and reviewer-only readings are labelled in the notes. Quotations taken from another copy of The Brenner Debate (1985) were withdrawn by the Brenner research and are not used. Optional and weak items are left out (see edges_considered_not_proposed in the capitalismdebates draft). The debate's own arrows follow the sciencewars pattern: fields and persons contribute to it, and its named critics are drawn from it to the person they answer.

edge_1050.relationship: Broadberry and Gupta place the advanced parts of Asia with Europe's stagnating periphery on wages and prices (2006); Mokyr finds coal and ghost acreage 'not incorrect but by itself cannot do the job' (2002); Vries finds differences, not 'surprising resemblances' (2009); Allen and colleagues dispute Chinese–English urban real-wage parity (2011); Broadberry, Guan and Li place divergence between leading regions around 1700 (2021)
edge_1050.map_label: Knowledge, wages, the state and regional GDP, 2002–2021
edge_1050.evidence_note: This arrow represents named interventions within the debate entry, not a verdict of it; the entry includes Pomeranz and his allies, and each intervention establishes something different. Broadberry and Gupta (EHR 59:1, 2006; summary and pp. 2–3 read), on wages and prices: "Contrary to the claims of Pomeranz, Parthasarathi, and other 'world historians', the prosperous parts of Asia between 1500 and 1800 look similar to the stagnating southern, central, and eastern parts of Europe … The 'great divergence' … was already well underway before 1800" (p. 2). Mokyr ('The Enduring Riddle of the European Miracle', author's draft, October 2002, pp. 2–4 read), on knowledge: of coal, 'the argument can be and has been overdone'; of ghost acreage, 'this argument is not incorrect but by itself cannot do the job'; Pomeranz 'does not confront the "Needham Questions" squarely'; 'the sheer enormity of the gap requires a better explanation than historical luck (European discoveries) or geographical accident (coal, proximity to America)'. Vries ('A World of Surprising Resemblances?', 2009, pp. 35–38, 47–48 read), on agriculture and the state: 'I would not call that a "surprising resemblance"' (p. 38); 'Coal and colonies definitely were fundamental in the Rise of the West. But reference to them cannot suffice to explain it' (p. 48). Allen, Bassino, Ma, Moll-Murata and van Zanden (EHR 2011, read pp. 8–9, 29–31), on urban real wages: 'our findings also dispute the revisionists’ claim that the advanced parts of China, such as the Yangzi Delta, were on a par with England'; 'Adam Smith’s pessimism looks closer to the truth than the revisionists’ optimism' (p. 31); they also find Chinese urban wages on a par with central and southern Europe, against the 'rise of the west' literature (pp. 30–31). Broadberry, Guan and Li (JEH 2021, read pp. 958–959), on regional GDP per capita: 'The Great Divergence thus began around 1700, earlier than originally suggested by the California School, but later than implied by earlier writers' (p. 958); the qualified chronology is theirs alone. None endorses Huang's involution, whose dispute with Pomeranz is drawn on its own arrows. Revision 1.145 moved this arrow from economic to the debate entry capitalismdebates, and moved Brenner and Isett's 2002 critique to its own arrow (robert_brenner → kenneth_pomeranz), as this note had foreseen.

edge_407.relationship: Drescher contests the economic-decline explanation for 1807 abolition (1977, in the publisher's description of Econocide); Eltis and Engerman judge the growth linkages of slavery to British industry small (2000, as Hilt reports)
edge_407.map_label: Decline and abolition disputed; slavery’s weight questioned, 1977–2000
edge_407.evidence_note: In its publisher's description (the monograph is unread), Econocide (1977) emphasizes continued economic potential and public mobilization. This is one named intervention within economic/abolition debates, not the entire field’s verdict or a test of all Williams’s propositions. Full statistical evidence remains unchecked. The arrow concerns the decline-and-abolition and growth-linkage questions; slave-derived wealth in British society is carried by Hall's edges. Revision 1.145 moved this arrow from economic to the debate entry capitalismdebates and added further named readers. Drescher's own retrospect ('Capitalism and Slavery after Fifty Years', 1997, opening read) names 'the Williams-Drescher debate' and calls the book 'a classic' that reoriented the subject. Eltis and Engerman (JEH 2000, unread; mediated) concluded, as Hilt reports (JEH 2017, p. 516), that 'the total value added and growth-inducing linkages of the British slave trade and Caribbean slave plantations were not particularly large'; Burnard and Riello (JGH 2020, p. 226) quote Solow's middle position, that slavery 'did not cause the Industrial Revolution but played an active role in its pattern and timing' (1987, p. 72), and judge that Williams's 'contemporary defenders … use Williams for historical perspectives he never considered' (p. 227).

edge_478.evidence_note: Sweezy pp. 134–137 questions breadth and regional transfer; Takahashi pp. 313–315 calls for fuller French/German engagement while developing production-relation analysis. Two distinct interventions, not a united school or complete reading of both critiques. Revision 1.145: Sweezy's critique, now read in full (pp. 134–157), was offered as a correction from within: 'no theory which fails to take into account the factors which Dobb stresses … can be regarded as correct' (p. 142); his own model made feudalism 'a system of production for use' (p. 136) and the growth of trade 'the root cause' of its decline (p. 142).

edge_899.evidence_note: Pomeranz's own argument, The Great Divergence (2000), introduction (pp. 3–27 read; later-edition pagination). He takes 'Why wasn’t England the Yangzi Delta?' as seriously as 'Why wasn’t the Yangzi Delta England?' and argues 'that Europe, too, could have wound up on an “east Asian,” labor-intensive path', a result avoided through 'sharp discontinuities, based on both fossil fuels and access to New World resources' (p. 13). 'Constraints connected to energy, and ultimately to quantities of land (particularly the shrinking forests of core areas throughout Eurasia), were a far more important looming impediment to further growth' than capital (p. 19). The Atlantic trade mattered for 'how much they relieved the strain on Europe’s supply of what was truly scarce: land and energy', and 'the fruits of overseas exploitation were probably roughly as important to at least Britain’s economic transformation as its epochal turn to fossil fuels' (p. 23). The book uses 'the fruits of overseas coercion' to explain the difference from China and Japan, 'not the whole of that development' (p. 4). Cooper's 2000 review (read in full) summarises it in the same year: 'Europe had more institutional slack, easier access to coal (which was crucial, in the author's view), and cheap imports of sugar and cotton harvested by slaves in its New World colonies', and objects that Pomeranz 'relies heavily on plausible guesstimates'. The earlier Making of a Hinterland (1993) already argued, in the publisher's description, 'that the development of certain regions entailed the systematic underdevelopment of other regions'; Bianco (1996, p. 243, read) notes that it 'ne sépare jamais l'enquête régionale du débat théorique', including Huang's involution model. A contribution, not a founding: earlier arguments from colonial extraction (Williams 1944, Frank 1969, Amin 1974) are cited at p. 3, n. 2, and he notes parallels with Sugihara (p. 12). Huang's 2002 critique and Pomeranz's reply are later readings, not evidence for this edge. Revision 1.144: the critiques now have their own arrows (philip_huang → kenneth_pomeranz; economic → kenneth_pomeranz, which revision 1.145 moved to capitalismdebates → kenneth_pomeranz, with Brenner and Isett drawn separately as robert_brenner → kenneth_pomeranz). Pomeranz restated the timing in 2003: "a gathering consensus, pace Huang, about the timing of that divergence" (JAS 62:1, p. 179, read). Catherine Hall reads the coal-and-colonies argument as part of "a modified version of Williams’s thesis amongst economic historians": "Pomeranz sees the Atlantic slave-economy and the availability of coal as the two complementary factors allowing Britain to expand" (History Workshop Journal 78, 2014, p. 24, read).

text_revisions.old: Dobb gives priority to production relations while allowing trade to interact with conflict. Sweezy questions definition and regional transfer; Takahashi develops labour-form analysis and challenges limited coverage. These are distinct positions.
text_revisions.new: Dobb gives priority to production relations while allowing trade to interact with conflict. Sweezy questions definition and regional transfer; Takahashi develops labour-form analysis and challenges limited coverage. These are distinct positions. Brenner's 1976 article reopened the question around property relations; Hilton (1985) called the ensuing debate a continuation of this one, now held with its sequels in the debate entry capitalismdebates.
text_revisions.reason: Revision 1.145: Brenner joins the strand (see strand_list_additions).

text_revisions.old: The division of labor defines the historical unit, with external arenas distinguished from internal exchange. Coerced labor can belong to capitalism in Wallerstein’s contested account.
text_revisions.new: The division of labor defines the historical unit, with external arenas distinguished from internal exchange. Coerced labor can belong to capitalism in Wallerstein’s contested account. Brenner (1977) charged Wallerstein, with Frank and Sweezy, with a 'neo-Smithian' Marxism that made trade the source of capitalism.
